title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
lead: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all the same kind of wave, and what separates one band from the next is nothing but frequency. This section states the relation $\kc = \kf\klam$ that ties a frequency to a wavelength, lays the whole spectrum out on those two scales, and then walks it band by band: how each one is produced, what it is used for, how far it penetrates, and what it does to living tissue.
objectives: List three “rules of thumb” that apply to the different frequencies along the electromagnetic spectrum.
Explain why the higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength of an electromagnetic wave.
Draw a simplified electromagnetic spectrum, indicating the relative positions, frequencies, and spacing of the different types of radiation bands.
List and explain the different methods by which electromagnetic waves are produced across the spectrum.
summary_html:
• The relationship among the speed of propagation, wavelength, and frequency for any wave is given by $\kvw = \kf\klam$, so that for electromagnetic waves, $$\kc = \kf\klam,$$ where $\kf$ is the frequency, $\klam$ is the wavelength, and $\kc$ is the speed of light.
  • The electromagnetic spectrum is separated into many categories and subcategories, based on the frequency and wavelength, source, and uses of the electromagnetic waves.
  • Any electromagnetic wave produced by currents in wires is classified as a radio wave, the lowest frequency electromagnetic waves. Radio waves are divided into many types, depending on their applications, ranging up to microwaves at their highest frequencies.
  • Infrared radiation lies below visible light in frequency and is produced by thermal motion and the vibration and rotation of atoms and molecules. Infrared’s lower frequencies overlap with the highest-frequency microwaves.
  • Visible light is largely produced by electronic transitions in atoms and molecules, and is defined as being detectable by the human eye. Its colors vary with frequency, from red at the lowest to violet at the highest.
  • Ultraviolet radiation starts with frequencies just above violet in the visible range and is produced primarily by electronic transitions in atoms and molecules.
  • X-rays are created in high-voltage discharges and by electron bombardment of metal targets. Their lowest frequencies overlap the ultraviolet range but extend to much higher values, overlapping at the high end with gamma rays.
  • Gamma rays are nuclear in origin and are defined to include the highest-frequency electromagnetic radiation of any type.
notes: The link to the PhET simulation Color Vision is left out, as the links to the publisher’s interactive content are throughout, and twelve of the module’s twenty-four problems have no keyed answer and are left out with it, among them the AM and FM wavelength ranges, the frequency range of visible light, the two radar timing problems, the light-year problem and the TV reception antenna, whose image is therefore not kept either.

Twelve of the twenty-four problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the AM and FM wavelength ranges, the frequency range of visible light, the frequency of 15.0 μm infrared, the radar echo at $6\times 10^{-5}$ s, the travel time of X-rays over 1 mm and 1 cm, the time for sunlight to reach the Earth, the light-year conversions, the electromagnetic wave of a beating heart, the MRI wavelength range, the TV reception antenna, the lunar reflector and the ratio of the frequencies the eye and the ear respond to. All twelve conceptual questions are unkeyed in the book and are kept as open items with an AI-marked suggested approach. Of the four AP items, this module’s ordering by wavelength is keyed and set as a graded choice, and its item on vision in the radio band is unkeyed and kept open; the other two are printed in 24.2, need $\kc = \kf\klam$, and are set here with that section named as their source. The module prints no Check Your Understanding box, so nothing is set inline. Numeric answers accept 2% tolerance.

exercises.prompt: If you live in a region that has a particular TV station, you can sometimes pick up some of its audio portion on your FM radio receiver. Explain how this is possible. Does it imply that TV audio is broadcast as FM?

answer.solution: The TV audio signal is broadcast as FM, and the VHF channels lie on both sides of the FM radio band: channels 2 to 6 use 54 to 88 MHz and channels 7 to 13 use 174 to 222 MHz, while the FM band runs from 88 to 108 MHz. A receiver tuned to the edge of its own band can resonate with the audio carrier of a nearby channel, and since that carrier is modulated in frequency in exactly the way an FM station is, the receiver’s circuitry turns it back into sound. So yes, picking the audio up on an FM receiver does imply that the TV audio is broadcast as FM.

exercises.prompt: Explain why people who have the lens of their eye removed because of cataracts are able to see low-frequency ultraviolet.

answer.solution: The retina responds to the lowest ultraviolet frequencies, but that radiation does not normally reach it, because the cornea and the lens absorb it first. When the lens is removed, the ultraviolet that the lens would have taken up passes through to the retina instead, and the retina answers it as it answers visible light.

exercises.prompt: How do fluorescent soap residues make clothing look “brighter and whiter” in outdoor light? Would this be effective in candlelight?

answer.solution: A fluorescent residue absorbs ultraviolet and gives the energy back out at visible wavelengths, so in sunlight the cloth returns more visible light than falls on it and looks brighter and whiter than plain cloth. A candle flame is much cooler than the Sun and sends out almost no ultraviolet, so there is nothing for the residue to absorb and the effect would not be seen by candlelight.

exercises.prompt: Give an example of resonance in the reception of electromagnetic waves.

answer.solution: A radio receiver is tuned so that its circuit has the same resonant frequency as the carrier wave of the station wanted, and it responds strongly to that one frequency while rejecting the many others arriving at its antenna. The antenna itself is a second example: a linear antenna answers best when it is half a wavelength long, because a standing wave of current then fits along it.

exercises.prompt: Illustrate that the size of details of an object that can be detected with electromagnetic waves is related to their wavelength, by comparing details observable with two different types (for example, radar and visible light or infrared and X-rays).

answer.solution: Take a 500 MHz radar and green light of 550 nm. The radar has a wavelength of λ = c/f = 0.600 m, so it maps the shape of an aircraft or a hillside but cannot make out anything much smaller than half a meter, while green light has a wavelength about a million times shorter and shows detail down to a fraction of a micrometer, which is why an optical microscope can show a cell and radar cannot. The same comparison holds between infrared, whose wavelengths run from about 0.74 μm to 300 μm, and X-rays, whose wavelengths can be less than 0.01 nm and which are therefore scattered by the spacings inside a crystal.

exercises.prompt: Why don’t buildings block radio waves as completely as they do visible light?

answer.solution: A radio wave is meters to hundreds of meters long, so a building and its openings are not large compared with the wavelength and the wave passes around and through them much as an ocean wave passes a rock. Visible light has a wavelength shorter than a micrometer, so a wall is enormous beside it and blocks it as a solid obstacle. On top of that, brick, wood and plaster are largely transparent at radio frequencies and opaque at visible ones.

exercises.prompt: Make a list of some everyday objects and decide whether they are transparent or opaque to each of the types of electromagnetic waves.

answer.solution: Window glass is transparent to visible light and to infrared of the nearest wavelengths, largely opaque to ultraviolet, and transparent to radio waves. Human skin is opaque to visible light and to ultraviolet but transparent to X-rays, which is what makes a shadow X-ray image possible. A brick wall is opaque to visible light and fairly transparent to radio. The metal grid in the door of a microwave oven is opaque to microwaves, whose wavelength is far larger than the holes, and transparent to visible light, whose wavelength is far smaller. Air is transparent to visible light and to radio, and takes up a good deal of infrared through its carbon dioxide and water.

exercises.prompt: Your friend says that more patterns and colors can be seen on the wings of birds if viewed in ultraviolet light. Would you agree with your friend? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: Your friend is right about the patterns. Many birds carry markings that reflect ultraviolet strongly in places where the plumage looks plain to us, and other birds can see those frequencies, so an ultraviolet image shows structure that visible light does not. It is not right to call them colors in the ordinary sense, though: the eye assigns no color to ultraviolet, and a picture of it has to be printed in visible colors that stand for the ultraviolet rather than being it.

exercises.prompt: The rate at which information can be transmitted on an electromagnetic wave is proportional to the frequency of the wave. Is this consistent with the fact that laser telephone transmission at visible frequencies carries far more conversations per optical fiber than conventional electronic transmission in a wire? What is the implication for ELF radio communication with submarines?

answer.solution: It is consistent. Visible light has a frequency of about 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz and the signals carried on a wire have frequencies millions of times lower, so a single fiber can carry a correspondingly larger number of conversations at once. The implication for ELF is the opposite one: at about 1 kHz the frequency is lower again by eleven powers of ten, so very little information can be sent per unit time and messages to a submerged submarine have to be short and slow.

exercises.prompt: Give an example of energy carried by an electromagnetic wave.

answer.solution: Sunlight warms whatever absorbs it: about half the solar energy arriving at the Earth is in the infrared and most of the rest is visible, and on average half of what arrives is absorbed by the Earth. A microwave oven is a second example, where microwaves at 2.45 GHz are absorbed by the water in food and raise its temperature.

exercises.prompt: In an MRI scan, a higher magnetic field requires higher frequency radio waves to resonate with the nuclear type whose density and location is being imaged. What effect does going to a larger magnetic field have on the most efficient antenna to broadcast those radio waves? Does it favor a smaller or larger antenna?

answer.solution: A larger magnetic field raises the resonant frequency, and since λ = c/f a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength. The most efficient linear antenna is half a wavelength long, so the antenna wanted gets shorter as the field is raised: a larger field favors a smaller antenna.

exercises.prompt: Laser vision correction often uses an excimer laser that produces 193-nm electromagnetic radiation. This wavelength is extremely strongly absorbed by the cornea and ablates it in a manner that reshapes the cornea to correct vision defects. Explain how the strong absorption helps concentrate the energy in a thin layer and thus give greater accuracy in shaping the cornea. Also explain how this strong absorption limits damage to the lens and retina of the eye.

answer.solution: Strong absorption means the radiation is taken up within a very short distance of the surface, so all the energy of a burst is delivered to a layer a fraction of a micrometer thick rather than being spread through the depth of the cornea. That is what lets the surgeon remove a controlled thickness at a time and shape the cornea accurately. The same strong absorption protects what lies behind: almost nothing of the 193 nm radiation survives the first layer of the cornea, so the lens and the retina receive no appreciable dose.

exercises.prompt: The correct ordering from least to greatest wavelength is:

options: ELF, FM radio, microwaves, infrared, red, green, ultraviolet, x-ray, gamma ray
ELF, FM radio, microwaves, infrared, green, red, ultraviolet, x-ray, gamma ray
gamma ray, x-ray, ultraviolet, red, green, infrared, microwaves, FM radio, ELF
gamma ray, x-ray, ultraviolet, green, red, infrared, microwaves, FM radio, ELF
answer.hint: Wavelength runs the opposite way to frequency, and within the visible band red has the longest wavelength of all.
answer.solution: (d). The shortest wavelengths belong to the gamma rays and the longest to ELF, so the list must start at the gamma-ray end and finish at ELF, which rules out (a) and (b). Within the visible band violet and green are shorter than red, so green must come before red, which rules out (c) and leaves (d).

exercises.prompt: Describe how our vision would be different if we could see energy in what we define as the radio spectrum.

answer.solution: We would see over a far wider range of wavelengths than the narrow strip we see now, but we would see it much less sharply, because the smallest detail a wave can resolve is set by its wavelength and a radio wavelength is meters rather than fractions of a micrometer. Broadcast antennas, mobile phones, power lines and ordinary circuits would all shine, since each of them radiates in that range, and we could probably tell AM from FM and from other radio frequencies as we now tell one color from another. Walls would be far less of an obstacle, since buildings do not block radio waves as completely as they block light.

exercises.prompt: If an electromagnetic wave is described as having a frequency of 3 GHz, what are its period and wavelength (in a vacuum)?

answer.hint: The period is one over the frequency, and the wavelength is the speed of light divided by the frequency.
answer.solution: (b). The period is T = 1/f = 1/(3 × 10⁹ Hz) = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ s, and the wavelength is λ = c/f = (3.00 × 10⁸ m/s)/(3 × 10⁹ Hz) = 0.10 m, which is 10 cm.

exercises.prompt: A wave is travelling through a medium until it hits the end of the medium and there is nothing but vacuum beyond. What happens to a mechanical wave? Electromagnetic wave?

answer.hint: Ask which of the two kinds of wave needs something to travel in.
answer.solution: (a). A mechanical wave is a disturbance of a medium, and with no medium beyond the boundary there is nothing for it to travel in, so it is turned back. An electromagnetic wave is a disturbance of the electric and magnetic fields themselves and needs no medium at all, so it carries on into the vacuum.

exercises.prompt: (a) Two microwave frequencies are authorized for use in microwave ovens: 900 and 2560 MHz. Calculate the wavelength of each. (b) Which frequency would produce smaller hot spots in foods due to interference effects?

answer.solution: (a) 33.3 cm (900 MHz), 11.7 cm (2560 MHz). (b) The microwave oven with the smaller wavelength would produce smaller hot spots in foods, corresponding to the one with the frequency 2560 MHz.

exercises.prompt: A radio station utilizes frequencies between commercial AM and FM. What is the frequency of a 11.12-m-wavelength channel?
Combing your hair leads to excess electrons on the comb. How fast would you have to move the comb up and down to produce red light?

answer.hint: An accelerating charge radiates at the frequency at which it is moved, so ask what frequency red light has.

exercises.prompt: Approximately what is the smallest detail observable with a microscope that uses ultraviolet light of frequency $1.20\times 10^{15}\ \text{Hz}$?

answer.hint: The smallest detail is about one wavelength.
answer.solution: $\klam = \frac{\kc}{\kf} = \frac{3.00\times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}}{1.20\times 10^{15}\ \text{Hz}} = 2.50\times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}$

exercises.prompt: Some radar systems detect the size and shape of objects such as aircraft and geological terrain. Approximately what is the smallest observable detail utilizing 500-MHz radar?

answer.hint: The smallest detail a probe resolves is about its wavelength.

exercises.prompt: If you wish to detect details of the size of atoms (about $1\times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$) with electromagnetic radiation, it must have a wavelength of about this size. (a) What is its frequency? (b) What type of electromagnetic radiation might this be?

answer.hint: Use $\kf = \kc/\klam$, then read the answer off the spectrum.
answer.solution: (a) $\kf = \frac{\kc}{\klam} = \frac{3.00\times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}}{1\times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}} = 3\times 10^{18}\ \text{Hz}$. (b) X-rays.

exercises.prompt: A certain 50.0-Hz AC power line radiates an electromagnetic wave having a maximum electric field strength of 13.0 kV/m. (a) What is the wavelength of this very low frequency electromagnetic wave? (b) What is its maximum magnetic field strength?

parts.hint: Use $\klam = \kc/\kf$ for the first part and $\kEfo/\kBmago = \kc$, from Section 24.2, for the second.

exercises.prompt: (a) The ideal size (most efficient) for a broadcast antenna with one end on the ground is one-fourth the wavelength ($\klam/4$) of the electromagnetic radiation being sent out. If a new radio station has such an antenna that is 50.0 m high, what frequency does it broadcast most efficiently? Is this in the AM or FM band? (b) Discuss the analogy of the fundamental resonant mode of an air column closed at one end to the resonance of currents on an antenna that is one-fourth their wavelength.

answer.hint: If the antenna is a quarter of a wavelength, the wavelength is four times its height.
answer.solution: (a) $1.50\times 10^{6}$ Hz, which is in the AM band. (b) The resonance of currents on an antenna that is 1/4 their wavelength is analogous to the fundamental resonant mode of an air column closed at one end, since the tube also has a length equal to 1/4 the wavelength of the fundamental oscillation.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the frequency of the 193-nm ultraviolet radiation used in laser eye surgery? (b) Assuming the accuracy with which this EM radiation can ablate the cornea is directly proportional to wavelength, how much more accurate can this UV be than the shortest visible wavelength of light?

parts.hint: For the second part take the shortest visible wavelength as 380 nm and form the ratio.

answer.solution: (a) $1.55\times 10^{15}$ Hz. (b) The shortest wavelength of visible light is 380 nm, so that the ratio is 380 nm / 193 nm = 1.97. In other words, the UV radiation is 97% more accurate than the shortest wavelength of visible light, or almost twice as accurate.

exercises.prompt: Conversations with astronauts on lunar walks had an echo that was used to estimate the distance to the Moon. The sound spoken by the person on Earth was transformed into a radio signal sent to the Moon, and transformed back into sound on a speaker inside the astronaut’s space suit. This sound was picked up by the microphone in the space suit (intended for the astronaut’s voice) and sent back to Earth as a radio echo of sorts. If the round-trip time was 2.60 s, what was the approximate distance to the Moon, neglecting any delays in the electronics?

answer.hint: The radio signal covers the distance twice in the round-trip time, and it travels at the speed of light.

exercises.prompt: Radar is used to determine distances to various objects by measuring the round-trip time for an echo from the object. (a) How far away is the planet Venus if the echo time is 1000 s? (b) What is the echo time for a car 75.0 m from a Highway Police radar unit? (c) How accurately (in nanoseconds) must you be able to measure the echo time to an airplane 12.0 km away to determine its distance within 10.0 m?

parts.hint: Each echo time covers the distance twice, at the speed of light.

exercises.prompt: (a) Calculate the rate in watts at which heat transfer through radiation occurs (almost entirely in the infrared) from $1.0\ \text{m}^{2}$ of the Earth’s surface at night. Assume the emissivity is 0.90, the temperature of the Earth is $15^\circ\text{C}$, and that of outer space is 2.7 K. (b) Compare the intensity of this radiation with that coming to the Earth from the Sun during the day, which averages about $800\ \text{W/m}^2$, only half of which is absorbed. (c) What is the maximum magnetic field strength in the outgoing radiation, assuming it is a continuous wave?

parts.hint: Part (a) is the radiated power of Chapter 14; part (c) needs the intensity of Section 24.4.

parts.part: (b) as a percent of the absorbed sunlight
